newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin to meet top ministers, cabinet takes shape.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin to meet top ministers, cabinet takes shape.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin will meet his prime minister and two other top ministers on Wednesday at a session which could complete Russia's government reshuffle.

Presidential press secretary Sergei Yastrzhembsky said on Tuesday that Yeltsin would discuss wage delays at the meeting with Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and his two first deputy prime ministers, Anatoly Chubais and Boris Nemtsov.
"I consider the situation with the mass delays in wage payments unbearable," Yastrzhembsky, speaking at a news briefing, quoted Yeltsin as saying.
The government scheduled a news conference for after the meeting. Itar-Tass news agency said the final names in the government team were likely to be revealed.
"The line-up of the new cabinet is expected to be announced at the news conference," Tass said.

Chernomyrdin, Chubais and Nemtsov were expected to take part in the news conference. The prime minister said on Monday that he planned to propose his choices for most of the remaining cabinet vacancies to Yeltsin on Wednesday.

"In the last two weeks, large parts of the government have worked round-the-clock in connection with the reorganisation of the government and the union protests on March 27," government spokesman Igor Shabdurasulov told reporters.
Trade unions have called a nationwide day of protest on Thursday against delays of up to several months in payment of wages in many state sectors.

Chubais and Nemtsov are the two most prominent appointees in the new government, the top ranks of which were announced last week. Both have pledged to speed up economic reforms and Nemtsov has promised to restructure powerful Russian monopolies.
Yastrzhembsky made clear Yeltsin had been considering the root causes of the planned protests.

He said the president had demanded better coordination of efforts to wipe out wage delays and called for moves to defend the interests of the millions of Russians who invested money in saving systems which later collapsed.
